justification: No demonstrable factual error found; the article is clearly and substantially ahead of every comparable page I could fetch, because it is the only one of the four that compiles and runs a real diamond-inheritance rejection, reproduces a genuine silent regression with matching wrong output, and then reruns the corrected design to show the number becomes right — none of Wikipedia's, ThoughtWorks', or even the GoF book's own treatments of this question go past abstract illustration. Independent verification performed directly, not just trusted from the article: (1) ran `node tools/run-code.mjs` three consecutive times from PowerShell — PASS, blocks=13, executed=7, byte-identical each time, matching the writer's claim with no flakiness; (2) compiled the exact `sealed class Wyvern : Archer, FlyingGoblin` diamond attempt myself on .NET 10.0.401 via `dotnet run`, and got `error CS1721: Class 'Wyvern' cannot have multiple base classes: 'Archer' and 'FlyingGoblin'` — this is a verbatim match to the quoted diagnostic text and code; (3) hand-traced the gas-hazard 'silent bug' arithmetic against the article's own hazard rules (Lava 10, Gas 6) over the five-tile path and confirmed Goblin/Archer both land on hp 8, FlyingGoblin correctly lands on hp 18 (two gas hits only), and Wyvern's stale hand-copied override, which does nothing for any hazard, correctly produces hp 30 (no damage at all) — the demonstrated bug is real, not staged; the companion 'does a cast change the answer' exercise is also correct C# (virtual dispatch runs off the run-time type regardless of the static reference type, so neither an Archer- nor Enemy-typed reference reaches base-class gas handling once Wyvern overrides CrossTile — I re-derived this independently and it holds); (4) hand-traced the composed version and confirmed Wyvern now shares the single `flying` IMovement instance with Flying Goblin and both correctly land on hp 18, which is the actual fix, not just a rewrite; (5) checked the writer's decision not to invoke LSP and judge it sound on independent analysis: Enemy.CrossTile is declared virtual specifically to admit different per-subclass hazard behavior, so the base class makes no formal promise about what any override must compute: no precondition is strengthened, no invariant Enemy declares is broken (Hp only ever decreases, and does so validly under Wyvern's override too), and every caller holding any Enemy/Archer/Wyvern-typed reference gets consistent, non-throwing, type-correct dispatch — the cast exercise the article includes is itself evidence of this, since the wrong output is identical regardless of which supertype reference is used, which is exactly what you'd expect from a correctly-dispatching but numerically-stale override, not from a broken substitutability contract. The actual defect is that FlyingGoblin and Wyvern are unrelated siblings with no shared type capturing 'is a flying thing,' so there are two independent, un-synchronized copies of the same domain rule — a duplication/fragile-base-class problem, not an LSP violation, since LSP is about a subtype breaking a contract its supertype actually promises, and nothing here does. This is a correct and appropriately conservative judgment call; a weaker article would have reached for LSP as a buzzword and been wrong to. (6) Confirmed the exception-hierarchy claims by reflection (`typeof(ArgumentOutOfRangeException)` base-type walk on .NET 10 prints Object -> Exception -> SystemException -> ArgumentException -> ArgumentOutOfRangeException, i.e. ArgumentOutOfRangeException -> ArgumentException -> SystemException -> Exception as stated) and by fetching the cited ArgumentOutOfRangeException API page, whose own 'Inheritance' breadcrumb matches exactly; also compiled and ran the ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace / ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegative example myself and got the exact printed output shown. The claim that every thrown .NET object must derive from System.Exception is correct for the modern CLR/C# and is reasonably supported by the fetched exceptions-handling doc ('an exception is an object that inherits from the System.Exception class'). (7) Fetched the CS1721 docs page directly: its message template and 'a class can implement any number of interfaces' guidance match the article's paraphrase. (8) The GoF 'Favor object composition over class inheritance' quote could not be checked against the original book text (no accessible full-text copy found, consistent with the writer's own disclosed limitation); it is however one of the most widely and consistently quoted lines in the software-engineering literature, and I could not find any source that renders it differently — the writer's two-independent-secondary-source verification approach is a reasonable substitute given the constraint, and nothing found here contradicts it. (9) The M x A vs M + A combinatorics in the closing exercise are correct: full subclassing needs up to M x A classes (one per combination, since a class has only one 'extends' slot), the composed design needs M + A (one implementation per movement kind plus one per attack kind, combinations formed by constructor calls), adding a new attack kind costs M new classes under subclassing versus exactly 1 new class under composition, and at the game's current M=2, A=2 the two designs tie at 4 classes each exactly as the solution states. (10) The :::pitfall about shared behavior objects being safe only when stateless is accurate and the article's own IMovement/IAttack implementations (Walking, Flying, Melee, Ranged) hold no mutable state (Melee/Ranged's Damage is get-only, fixed at construction); Walking/Flying's DamageFor is a pure function of its argument. Two minor items keep this from a higher score rather than any error: the sentence 'A C# class extends exactly one other class, full stop' is an over-generalization of the same shape this project's own four-pillars review previously flagged as minor (System.Object itself has no base class, and the cited MS Learn page says only one, not exactly one) — precedent in this repo treats this pattern as a minor nit, not a capping factual error, and I follow that precedent here since it does not affect any conclusion the article draws. Second, the front-matter source explicitly cites GoF 'chapter 5 (Strategy)', but the sentence that actually names the Strategy pattern ('...is applying the Strategy pattern...') carries no inline [3] marker; [3] is used only once, earlier, for the 'favor composition' quote from chapter 1's content. Everything else checked out on independent reproduction, all five sources are real, accurately represented, and each is cited inline at least once.
